lessons.title: Let's Plant a Seed
objectives: Plant a seed and describe what it needs
Notice the first root and shoot
explanation: A seed is like a little lunchbox with a baby plant inside. When it gets water and warmth, it wakes up and starts to grow. This is called germination.
First a tiny root grows down into the soil to drink water. Then a green shoot grows up towards the light.
To keep growing, the plant needs water, sunlight, air and soil. Too much water can drown it, so water a little at a time.

story.title: Tara's Tiny Bean
story.text: Tara the tortoise planted a bean in a cup and waited. Nothing! Day two — nothing! "Be patient," whispered the soil. On day four, a tiny root peeked out, then a green shoot unfolded like a sleepy stretch. "Hello, little plant!" Tara smiled.

explanation: A garden is busy with helpers! Bees visit flowers and carry pollen, which helps plants make fruit and seeds.

lessons.title: Light or Dark?
objectives: Carry out a simple fair test on plant needs
Explain why plants need light
explanation: To find out what plants need, scientists do a fair test: they change only ONE thing and keep everything else the same.
Put one cress pot in a sunny place and one in a dark cupboard. Give them the same water, soil and pot. Only the light is different.
Plants in the dark grow pale, thin and floppy, stretching to find light. Plants in the light grow green and strong, because leaves use light to make food.

lessons.title: Which Part Are We Eating?
objectives: Identify which plant part common foods come from
Name important Indian food crops
prerequisites: Knows the parts of a plant
explanation: Almost everything we eat comes from plants. We eat roots (carrot, radish), stems (potato is an underground stem!, sugarcane), leaves (spinach, methi), flowers (cauliflower, broccoli), fruits (mango, tomato) and seeds (rice, wheat, dal).
Grains like rice, wheat and millets (jowar, bajra, ragi) are the seeds of grass plants. They give us energy.
Pulses — dals, chickpeas, rajma — are seeds too, and give us protein to grow strong.

context.text: A potato is a tuber: a swollen underground stem, not a root. It has "eyes" (buds) that can sprout new shoots.

lessons.title: The Pollen Journey
objectives: Name the main parts of a flower
Explain how pollination leads to seeds and fruit
explanation: Flowers have colourful petals to attract visitors. In the middle are the stamens, which make powdery pollen, and the pistil, which contains tiny eggs (ovules).

Pollination happens when pollen moves from a stamen to a pistil. Bees, butterflies, birds and even bats carry pollen as they feed on nectar. Some plants, like wheat and maize, are pollinated by the wind.
After pollination, the ovules become seeds and the part around them often grows into a fruit.

examples: Sunbirds pollinate many Indian flowers.

story.title: The Sunbird's Breakfast
story.text: A tiny purple sunbird darted to a red hibiscus and dipped its curved beak inside for sweet nectar. When it flew off, yellow pollen dusted its head. At the next flower, some pollen rubbed off onto the pistil. "Thank you for the breakfast," the bird chirped — and the flower began to make seeds.

lessons.title: How Seeds Travel
objectives: Describe four ways seeds are dispersed
Link seed features to their dispersal method
explanation: If all seeds fell right under the parent plant, they would compete for light and water. So plants have clever ways to spread their seeds.
Wind: light seeds with fluffy parachutes or wings float away (dandelion, maple). Animals: tasty fruits are eaten and seeds pass out elsewhere; hooked burrs cling to fur.
Water: coconuts float across seas. Bursting: some pods dry and explode, flinging seeds (balsam, peas).

lessons.title: The Leaf Kitchen
objectives: Describe photosynthesis in a word equation
Explain why photosynthesis matters for all life
explanation: Leaves are like kitchens. They take in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny holes, and water from the roots. Using energy from sunlight, the green pigment chlorophyll helps turn these into sugar (glucose) — the plant's food.
Oxygen is released as a by-product. Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → (light, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen.
Almost all food chains begin with photosynthesis, and much of the oxygen we breathe comes from plants and ocean algae.

story.title: Van Helmont's Willow
story.text: In the 1600s, Jan van Helmont planted a small willow in a weighed pot of soil and only watered it for five years. The tree gained over 70 kilograms, but the soil lost hardly any weight. He concluded the mass came from water. Later scientists found much of it came from carbon dioxide in the air — through photosynthesis.

lessons.title: Kharif and Rabi
objectives: Distinguish Kharif and Rabi crops
Explain how irrigation helps farming
prerequisites: Knows the monsoon and food crops
explanation: Indian farmers grow crops in two main seasons. Kharif crops are sown at the start of the monsoon (around June–July) and harvested in autumn: rice, maize, cotton, soybean, bajra.
Rabi crops are sown in winter (around October–November) and harvested in spring: wheat, mustard, gram (chana), barley.
Irrigation — supplying water through canals, wells, tanks or drip pipes — lets farmers grow crops when rain is not enough. Drip irrigation saves water by delivering it right to the roots.

examples: Punjab is known for Rabi wheat.

story.title: Two Harvests
story.text: Farmer Raju planted rice when the monsoon rains came, and harvested golden paddy in October. Then he sowed wheat for winter, watering it from his tube well. By spring, the wheat stood tall. "Two harvests a year," he told his grandson, "if we respect the seasons and use water wisely."

lessons.title: Xylem and Phloem
objectives: Describe the roles of xylem and phloem
Explain transpiration and factors affecting it
explanation: Plants have two transport systems. Xylem vessels carry water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves. Phloem carries sugars made in the leaves to all parts of the plant, including roots, fruits and growing tips.
Water evaporates from leaves through stomata — this is transpiration. As water leaves, more is pulled up the xylem like sucking through a straw.
Transpiration is faster when it is hot, dry, windy and bright. Plants can close stomata to save water when it is dry.

examples: A large tree can move hundreds of litres of water a day in hot weather.

lessons.title: Forests of India
objectives: Describe major forest types in India
Discuss traditional plant knowledge and scientific evidence
explanation: India has many forest types: tropical evergreen forests in the Western Ghats and Northeast, deciduous forests (with teak and sal) that shed leaves in the dry season, mangroves like the Sundarbans on coasts, and alpine meadows in the Himalayas.
Many communities protect sacred groves — patches of forest preserved for religious or cultural reasons. They often shelter rare plants and animals.

Traditional systems like Ayurveda use many plants, such as neem, tulsi and turmeric. Some uses have scientific support; others are still being studied. Science tests claims carefully, while respecting traditional knowledge as a source of ideas.

context.text: Sacred groves (such as devrai in Maharashtra and kavu in Kerala) are protected by local communities through traditional customs.
Turmeric's compound curcumin is widely researched; evidence for many health claims remains limited or mixed, so medical advice should come from qualified doctors.

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Limiting Factors
objectives: Explain limiting factors of photosynthesis
Compare photosynthesis and respiration
explanation: Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (with light energy). It occurs in chloroplasts in two linked stages: light-dependent reactions (capturing light energy) and the Calvin cycle (fixing carbon into sugar).
The rate depends on limiting factors: light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature. Whichever is in shortest supply limits the rate. Greenhouses raise yields by controlling these factors.
All living cells, including plant cells, carry out respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy. Plants photosynthesise only in light but respire all the time.

vocabulary.meaning: the factor in shortest supply that restricts a process's rate
releasing energy from glucose in cells

the light-independent stage fixing carbon dioxide

examples: At night, plants release CO₂ because respiration continues without photosynthesis.
Commercial greenhouses add CO₂ to boost tomato yields.

story.title: The Greenhouse Grower
story.text: A tomato grower in Nashik noticed that on bright winter days, adding more light did nothing. She tested raising the temperature slightly — yields jumped. "Temperature was my limiting factor," she noted. Understanding the science saved her money and energy.

activities.prompt: If light is plentiful but CO₂ is low, the limiting factor is…

activities.why: They respire all the time; photosynthesis happens only in light.

lessons.title: Evaluating the Green Revolution
objectives: Explain what the Green Revolution was and its effects
Evaluate benefits and costs using evidence
explanation: In the 1960s, India faced food shortages. The Green Revolution introduced high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, expanded irrigation, and increased use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Scientists such as M. S. Swaminathan played leading roles, building on Norman Borlaug's wheat research.
Wheat and rice production rose dramatically, helping India become largely self-sufficient in staple grains and reducing famine risk.

There were costs too: in some regions, groundwater depletion, soil degradation, pesticide overuse, and less crop diversity (fewer millets and pulses). Today, sustainable agriculture seeks to keep yields high while protecting soil, water and biodiversity.

context.text: India's wheat production rose from about 12 million tonnes in 1965 to over 20 million tonnes by 1970; groundwater decline in Punjab and Haryana is documented by government agencies.
Historians and economists debate how to weigh the Green Revolution's benefits against its environmental and social costs.

story.title: A Scientist's Two Concerns
story.text: M. S. Swaminathan helped bring high-yield wheat to India in the 1960s. Decades later, he warned that soil health and water use needed urgent care, and called for an "evergreen revolution" — productivity without ecological harm. He saw both the triumph and the challenge.
